newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia shares seen riding even higher on fund flow.
newsitem.headline: Russia shares seen riding even higher on fund flow.

text.p: A fast and furious flow of cash into the Russian equities market which has pushed up stocks over 40 percent this month is not stopping -- and neither will the Russian bull market, traders and analysts said on Friday.
"Senior decisions have been taken on a senior level with these big funds," said Lars Bergstrom, Managing Director of Alfred Berg investment bank in Moscow.
"The Americans are definitely ahead in terms of (investment) volumes, but I think we will see the big European money coming in later this year."
Daily volumes topped $75 million this week, three times the level previously considered healthy, testifying to an inflow of new money.
Shares hit yet another record on Friday, with the Russian Trading System 24-share index ending 1.21 percent higher at 291.98 against 189.85 on Christmas Day.
Utility Mosenergo, the bellwether of the market which traded at $1.580 midday on Friday, closed at $0.978 at Christmas.
But the Russian market, which the International Finance Corporation said returned 156 percent last year as the world's best performing emerging market, is still considered cheap.

"A couple of leading stocks (now) have price-to-sales ratios that on the surface look comparable to the West, but they don't reflect growth potential," said Jim Nail, head of research at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell (DMG).
Nail said he prefers price/sales rather than price/earnings ratios because Russian accounting standards throw up corporate profit figures which cannot be compared with those in the West.

He said actively traded utilities had price/sales ratios of about 1.2, comparable to British utilities, but growth potential for the Russian energy market made investment prospects completely different from those of the developed world.

The Russian oil sector had an unweighted p/s ratio of about 0.75, at least one third that of Western competitors, he said, and telecoms had an unweighted p/s of about 1.75, versus 2.5 in Latin America.
"There is some ridiculously cheap paper," said a Western fund manager.
Many investors say price growth among the half dozen shares which have led the New Year rally will slow down soon but investment flows will begin to seek out a second tier of shares.
Peter Halloran, Director of Equities at CS First Boston, said investors would target 10-15 second-tier shares, especially in telecoms and utilities, in the first quarter of the year.
Those stocks could skyrocket just like the first group of shares at the beginning of the year, he said.
"There is potential for comparable growth."
Nail said DMG predicts the Moscow Times Index, which has just topped 200, would hit 320 by the end of the year.
But correction fears still loom and traders say that some operators have tried to minimise their risks by taking profits in the afternoon, when U.S. buyers enter the market.
Analysts said that corrections were inevitable, and Halloran said that the market illiquidity was still a danger.
"Most of the new buyers are taking the buy-and-hold approach," he said.

But they said Russia had turned a corner and that capital would continue to flow into Russia as investors, no longer worried by political traumas that have dogged Russia, moved to the question of what shares to buy.

"The risk of investing is more of a mature market, where you have to pick the right stocks," said Bergstrom. "It is not a question of Russia going ahead or not because it will. It is now a question of business risk."
